Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang on Opus 5.5, the Claude Platform, and the engineering behind AI agents. As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday , the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang , heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. Preserving thinking blocks across turns helps address this, but a new requirement can also break a customer's existing harness. Katelyn also describes what being part of early access programs actually looks like in practice: Customers run evaluations in their own harnesses, report surprising behavior, and sometimes pass along less formal impressions. The useful part is not just a benchmark score: it is seeing the model in environments and tasks Anthropic's own products do not cover. items.title: Beyond the Evidence Coherence Trap: Agent-Driven Evidence Selection for Temporally Disordered Fake News Detection
items.summary: Fake news undermines public trust and the integrity of online information ecosystems. Temporally disordered fake news is especially elusive because it rearranges factual events into a false chronology. Individual events may remain factually valid even when their temporal relations are misrepresented. When similar events involving the same entity recur, retrieval may return semantically plausible evidence from the wrong period. Consequently, independent event verification may rely on locally coherent but temporally mismatched evidence and incorrectly validate the article. We call this the \textit{evidence coherence trap}. Because existing benchmarks rarely isolate this setting, we construct ChronoFake, a source-disjoint benchmark of 30,706 articles derived from temporally anchored real events. It distinguishes temporal manipulation from valid narration, including flashbacks. To address this, we propose DelSA, a \underline{D}ocument S\underline{el}ection \underline{S}elf-Updating \underline{A}gent that iteratively refines evidence selection during training and applies a frozen rulebook for one-pass evidence selection at inference. DelSA uses an LLM to characterize candidate evidence, while a verifier-trained reranker balances local relevance against timeline consistency. Finally, the classifier compares the article-implied chronology extracted by the LLM with the evidence-derived chronology to reveal global temporal conflicts. DelSA outperforms existing methods on ChronoFake, while remaining competitive on PolitiFact and GossipCop.

items.title: Coverage Under Contradiction: A Benchmark for Negation-Aware Retrieval
items.summary: Coverage-evaluation benchmarks quantify whether retrieved evidence covers the different pieces of information needed to satisfy an information need. Existing benchmarks mostly consider factual claims that may already be known to pretrained retrieval components, leaving open whether retrievers find corpus evidence when it contradicts those priors. We study how retrievers behave when their parametric knowledge and the information in a corpus disagree. To do so, we develop a process to augment a nugget-based coverage benchmark with controlled contradictions. For each nugget, we create a negated counterpart and edit its supporting documents to support that negation while preserving the context. Applying this process to CoverageBench, a benchmark measuring information coverage, we create CoverageBench-Negate, spanning six datasets and roughly 63,000 original-edited evidence pairs (one per nugget-document link). We attach rich construction metadata to every pair and additionally provide out-of-family LLM judgments over all pairs and a human audit of a sample. In baseline experiments, BM25 separates original from edited near-twin evidence substantially better than dense retrievers (Qwen3 and Jina), which stay near chance. We release the benchmark on Hugging Face Datasets (nuggets, documents, pairs) together with the construction materials, including the prompts used to create it.

items.title: Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 is now available on Google Cloud
items.summary:
Earlier this year, we introduced Gemini Robotics 2 — our next-generation intelligence layer enabling robots to think, act, and adapt in the physical world. At the core of this breakthrough is Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 (ER 2), a specialized Gemini model that serves as a robot’s high-level brain. Working across any robot embodiment — from stationary arms to full humanoids — Gemini Robotics ER 2 combines advanced spatial and temporal video understanding with long-horizon planning and built-in safety guardrails. This enables robots to converse naturally with humans, orchestrate low-level action models and hardware APIs, execute multi-minute tasks involving hundreds of decisions, and collaborate across multi-robot teams.

Today, we are bringing this same frontier embodied reasoning model to enterprise production environments: Gemini Robotics ER 2 is now available in public preview on the Gemini platform. For the first time, organizations can pair Google DeepMind’s latest embodied reasoning model for robotics with the enterprise-grade security, multi-agent orchestration, and end-to-end lifecycle management of Google Cloud — making it easier to simulate, evaluate, and deploy safe, adaptive physical AI at scale.

Powering physical agents for enterprise robotics

Gemini Robotics ER 2 transforms a robot into a physical agent. The model combines deep spatio-temporal reasoning and long-horizon planning, enabling robots to orchestrate steps to complete a task, self-correct, and generalize to novel situations. To build an agentic setup, developers can declare low-level control interfaces — like Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models or navigation APIs — as tools, and stream multimodal video, audio, or text directly into the model.

Here is what the model delivers for businesses building and operating robotics:

1. Physical task verification, understanding, and self-correction

In physical operations, a robot needs to know whether a step actually succeeded before moving on to the next one. Gemini Robotics ER 2 adapts to new and unfamiliar situations on the fly by reasoning over continuous video feeds. The model:

  • Classifies task progress into binary status, discrete categories, or continuous scores to improve real-time situational awareness and enable real-time adjustment or iteration on failed steps, without restarting an entire workflow.

  • Pinpoints the exact video frame where a critical event occurs (such as when to stop pouring a liquid) with 91.3% accuracy and a 0.96-second mean absolute frame distance, running at 4x the execution speed and a fraction of the compute cost of many larger model categories.

  • It advances our core spatial reasoning capability, including visual question answering and instrument reading. For example, it can read and interpret values across 10+ instrument categories including circular dials, sight glasses, digital displays, linear scales, rulers, and liquid thermometers directly from visual input.

2. One intelligence layer across any embodiments

Gemini Robotics ER 2 orchestrates robots of many shapes and sizes, scaling its intelligence from stationary arms and wheeled rovers to quadrupeds and complex forms. It also unlocks multi-robot collaboration, allowing different types of robots to share a semantic understanding of their workspace, divide labor, and hand off tasks to complete workflows a single machine could not do alone.

3. Agentic tool orchestration and natural language interaction

Gemini Robotics ER 2 thinks about what comes next while simultaneously orchestrating  actions. Developers can declare low-level control interfaces — such as VLA models, navigation APIs, or custom functions — as tools across simulation, real-world robot control, or human tele-operation. Gemini Robotics ER 2 can orchestrate navigation and manipulator movement APIs from natural language commands, allowing the robot to explain its approach while performing an action, and letting operators redirect it without using technical language.

4. Build safe, adaptive physical agents in Google Cloud

Developers and enterprise teams use the Gemini platform to simulate, orchestrate, and manage physical agents, which are then deployed to run directly on physical robots at the edge using Google Cloud's scalable infrastructure:

  • Simulate fast:  Test robot behaviors before touching hardware by running simulations in familiar environments like MuJoCo-Warp and NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Then generate synthetic scenarios with multimodal models and auto-label workcell imagery on the Gemini platform.

  • Train smart: Use Gemini Robotics ER 2's spatial pointing, moment finding, and progress classification to curate and label demonstration videos in Cloud Storage and BigQuery. Then train custom Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models through the Gemini platform, GKE, or Cluster Director.

  • Operate easily: Deploy Gemini Robotics ER 2 workflows on the Gemini platform with enterprise IAM, security controls, and built-in function calling. Offload latency-sensitive local workloads like SLAM and path planning to factory floors with Google Distributed Cloud, and stream fleet telemetry into BigQuery. Explore the full architecture in Google Cloud Physical AI solutions.

How customers are building with Gemini Robotics ER 2 in Gemini platform

“We’ve seen exponential growth in customers using AIVI-Learning every month, and Gemini Robotics ER 2 brings them even more value. Video changes what an inspection can be. Spot isn’t just checking whether something looks right in a moment in time, the ability to apply AI models to video opens a whole new world of possibilities.” 

Marco da Silva, VP and General Manager of Spot at Boston Dynamics

“DeepReach AI is the real-world skills engine for physical AI. Our hardware and AI platform capture how skilled people work all over the world, and turn it into data flywheel for model training. Gemini Robotics ER 2 gives us accurate task understanding of every recording, to help us find data that matters most — faster and at a far greater scale.” 

Chris Liu, Co-founder and CTO at DeepReach

“Advanced reasoning models have the potential to help robots interpret complex environments, plan actions and adapt to changing conditions, opening new possibilities for physical AI. Google’s Gemini Robotics ER 2 model represents an important step in this direction, and we’re excited to be working with Google on exploring how these emerging capabilities can shape the next generation of robotics compute platforms.” 

Barrie Mullins, Senior Director of Arm Total Design for Physical AI, at Arm

“We aim to accelerate materials R&D workflows so our scientists can test more ideas, faster. Most lab automation today relies on rigid scripts for single, isolated tasks. By using Gemini Robotics ER 2, we are giving our robots the visual and physical flexibility to work with our existing infrastructure - whether that’s reading a touchscreen on a legacy microwave reactor that has no API, balancing and loading a centrifuge, or moving samples safely through a busy lab. This is the next level that we aspire to reach. This brings us much closer to self-driving labs that can run full experimental campaigns from synthesis to separation, freeing our researchers to focus on thinking up new ideas for discovering new materials.”

Prof. Loh Xian Jun, Executive Director at ASTAR Institute of Materials Research and Engineering (ASTAR IMRE) and Executive Director of MARVEL-AI”

Get started with Gemini Robotics ER 2 in Gemini platform

Developers and enterprise teams can start building with Gemini Robotics ER 2 today in preview via Model Garden in Gemini platform.

  • Build in Gemini platform: Try in Agent Studio. Visit the Gemini Robotics ER 2 documentation and pricing.

  • Explore the Developer Guides: Check out sample code and bidirectional streaming guides in the Gemini API Robotics documentation.

  • Read the Research: Dive into the benchmarks and safety technical report in the Google DeepMind Gemini Robotics ER 2 announcement.

  • Explore Physical AI on Google Cloud: Visit cloud.google.com/solutions/physical-ai and cloud.google.com/ai to learn how Google Cloud infrastructure supports simulation, training, and deployment.

items.title: How to build evidence-grounded agent memory with OpenWiki and Graphs
items.summary: LangChain used OpenWiki, its open-source wiki compiler, and an evidence graph to build a persistent memory layer that preserves knowledge for agents to reuse across tasks. Learn how.
items.story_key: story|title:how to build evidence grounded agent memory with openwiki and graphs
items.content_excerpt: Agents working across an organization’s policies, manuals, wikis, tickets, and code must navigate knowledge scattered across systems and teams. Finding a relevant passage is only the start. They also need to determine which rules apply, what has changed, and how one source affects another. A persistent memory layer preserves knowledge and relationships for agents to reuse across tasks. Without it, agents often have to reconstruct that understanding on every question, making their work expensive and error-prone. This is especially challenging in banking and insurance, where policies and guidelines frequently amend or supersede one another. We tested OpenWiki , our open-source wiki compiler, as this memory layer. On questions requiring connections across sources, the wiki made the agent roughly 5x more accurate than search alone. Adding an evidence graph that connects wiki statements to supporting passages and links related sources improved accuracy a further 27% and doubled citation consistency. RAG pipelines often use semantic or hybrid search to retrieve isolated chunks, leaving agents to piece together how those chunks relate. We’ve explored improving retrieval with agentic RAG and graph-based metadata filtering , but finding relevant passages is only part of the work. Cross-source questions require tracing references, resolving conflicting rules, and understanding dependencies. Memory preserves that understanding so agents don’t have to rebuild it on every question. A compiled wiki provides that memory layer by synthesizing source material into linked pages that explain key concepts and their relationships. The wiki is updated as sources change, giving agents context they can reuse. OpenWiki , our open-source CLI built on Deep Agents , creates these wikis with citations back to the sources. We originally built it so coding agents wouldn’t have to rediscover architecture and code behavior on every task. Every OpenWiki statement rests on a claim , an assertion linked to supporting source lines and their hash. When those lines change, the hash changes, allowing OpenWiki to flag affected claims without a model call, saving on token costs and making staleness detection more deterministic. Only those claims go to a model for confirmation, revision, or retraction, allowing the memory layer to self-correct as its sources change. items.title: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3
items.story_key: story|title:build specialized multimodal models with lfm3
items.content_excerpt: LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs. LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B . The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens. Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device. Each model runs in transformers . The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports. Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card . Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20 . Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker , it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db ) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. I use Colima rather than Docker Desktop, and even then, removing another dependency from the path to a working database is welcome. Local setup is a small part of a human developer's week; an agent that repeatedly creates and tests environments encounters it over and over. Declarative schemas are the bigger idea. The familiar SQL workflow accumulates a history: create the schema, then migrate, migrate, migrate. A declarative representation gives the agent a description of the state you want, in files it can inspect and edit alongside the application. In the commentary, I compare this to a Terraform moment for the database. Put the desired state in Git and the agent can read it, change it, fork it and work against it as part of the repository. Humans get the same advantage: the backend becomes easier to understand without reconstructing its entire history. That is the part I like most abou

items.title: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
items.summary: Genie 4: our new world model unlocking unprecedented realism in real-time simulation.
items.story_key: story|title:genie 4 a new generation of world simulation
items.content_excerpt: Today, we are announcing Genie 4, our new world model, which unlocks unprecedented realism and improves real-time interactive simulation. Genie 4 is natively multimodal, enabling audio-like music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue to be simultaneously generated with the world. The Genie 4 model incorporates and builds on capabilities from the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models provide the complex reasoning needed to help maintain a simulation’s coherence and continuity. With this foundation, you can set an event in motion, and Genie 4 simulates what happens next: how the world responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak. Understanding and simulating the world is a crucial aspect of building AGI. Genie 4 advances our ability to create safe, infinitely variable simulations that can help with everything from developing training environments for robots and agents to unlocking the creation of new interactive experiences. We have started rolling Genie 4 out as a research preview for trusted testers — gathering feedback before we release it to consumers and developers, starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie here . Genie 4 delivers enhanced photorealism, fluid movement, and native audio. All accompanying sounds featured above are produced directly by Genie 4. The following are recordings of real-time interactions from Genie 4, where users use standard keyboard controls for navigation and camera control, and text prompts to steer the scene as it evolves. With Genie 4, you can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time — like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object — and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene. Between your inputs, Gemini also monitors and steers the scene to keep the world progressing cohesively. Prompt: Use the reference image as the exact first frame and visual basis for the scene. Preserve the same floating rectangular platform, weathered concrete edges, wild grasses, ferns, twisted small tree, warm glowing amber sphere, and the same middle-aged man in a loose brown suit playing a brass saxophone. items.title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
items.summary: In a randomized trial, professional analysts working with an AI coding agent went with the option the agent was randomly assigned to favor 86% of the time. We look at what this means for human oversight of AI-assisted work.
items.story_key: story|title:how ai agents shape experts judgment calls
items.content_excerpt: When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call. We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded. Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead. Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed. Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment. We don’t know how much this tells us about the real world. Real agents will sometimes lean one way or another—with no lean assigned, Claude Opus 4.8 made the same five choices in 112 out of 123 runs—but in this case we strengthened their preferences o

items.title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
items.story_key: story|title:can we trust llms to judge whether a research idea is novel
items.content_excerpt: Today we’re releasing Old Ideas, Novel Problems , a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets. At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. DataVoyager helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, AutoDiscovery generates and tests hypotheses, and Theorizer synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with Asta , these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas. But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work. That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge . Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate. Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline. If AI is going to play a larger role in scientific discovery, we need more dependable ways to tell whether it is actually proposing something new. items.title: How to Build Proactive, Always-On Agents with the Schedules SDK in Managed Deep Agents
items.summary: Most proactive agents run on a simple cron. Learn what scheduled runs unlock, from memory to smart triage, and how to add them to Managed Deep Agents.
items.story_key: story|title:how to build proactive always on agents with the schedules sdk in managed deep a
items.content_excerpt: Ever hear of the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon? It's when you learn a word for the first time, and suddenly start hearing it everywhere. I think the same principle applies in software engineering: You learn about a simple, but effective, design pattern, and then suddenly start seeing it everywhere. We're seeing this happen with proactive agents, where we've noticed that nearly all of your favorite emerging proactive agentic systems are powered by a very simple mechanism: Agent runs as cron tasks, leveraging a more than fifty-year old principle of operating systems for a very modern use case. The future belongs to proactive, always-on, ambient agents. Launches like Muse, Instinct, Dots, Claude Duet, Hone, and more reflect this. Crons power a few different capabilities that combine to make these agents proactive, personalized, and ambient — that is, they can perform tasks on their own, without being manually instructed. In this blog, we will go through the capabilities that crons unlock, the two core underlying parts you need in order to build agents like this, and then show examples of how you can do this in Managed Deep Agents . We’ve seen the impact crons can have. Proactivity is the new default for agent behaviour because of the breadth of new functions it unlocks. More than 70% of Managed Deepagent runs on LangSmith come from scheduled runs rather than a human typing a message. Crons, despite being a simple concept, unlock a few different behaviors that shape these proactive, always-on agents. Memory: A distinctive part of all these agents is that they remember facts about you over longer time horizons. Implementing this partially involves running a background job to condense previous conversations into a denser form of memory. This is colloquially called “dreaming”. Under the hood, this is just a cron that runs on some cadence (e.g. once a day) and updates long-term memory with any learnings from reflecting on the conversations. Proactiveness : Part of what makes these agents work is that they initiate communication about an idea that they think you may be interested in. Under the hood, the way that this works is there is some “idea” of what this agent should be accomplishing. For a general purpose agent, it may be as simple as being a good assistant: taking steps to anticipate what you need next, like flagging an upcoming deadline, following up on an open thread, or surfacing news related to your work. For specialized agents, like with Hone, the agent is

items.title: claude-code v2.1.312
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added oidc.user_id_claim to the Claude apps gateway, to identify people by an id_token claim other than sub, such as Microsoft Entra ID's oid
  • Added click to send: in fullscreen, clicking the "to send now" hint under a queued message sends it right away, as its key does
  • Fixed managed settings and organization policy not being fetched for the rest of the session after signing in from the VS Code extension
  • Fixed Claude overwriting a very large CLAUDE.md, rules file or @-included file in a subdirectory after seeing only its start; Write now asks Claude to read it all or edit in place
  • Fixed per-directory and paths: skills not being found after a Bash cd deeper into a git repository
  • Fixed a rare case where the first reply after resuming a session in the terminal could be missing the next time the session was resumed
  • Fixed a command with an invalid name stopping all commands from loading, which could leave claude -p with no output
  • Fixed the Read tool sometimes failing on PDF pages with "pdftoppm failed: Could not write image" when the clean-up of old session files ran at the same time
  • Fixed the spinner, OpenTelemetry effort values and transcripts naming a newly picked effort level during a task before the model applied it; they now show the level in force
  • Fixed the /model and /effort cache warning saying the re-read waits for your next message; a change made while Claude is working can trigger it sooner
  • Fixed some sessions showing as waiting on you when the last message only mentioned items waiting on you mid-sentence
  • Fixed agent view restoring input text on the next launch after it was cleared with Ctrl+C just before exiting
  • Fixed agent view reopening in shell mode after exiting with Ctrl+D from an empty ! input
  • Fixed vim mode d, c and y with a gj or gk count larger than the lines left deleting or copying text; like Vim, they now only move the cursor
  • Fixed /verify showing a long description meant for Claude in /help and the / command menu instead of a short one
  • Improved the prompt's effort indicator: a change made mid-task now says it may wait for your next message, and the note clears when it no longer applies
  • Improved WebFetch errors in cloud sessions: a host that does not resolve is now explained as possibly outside the allowed network domains, so Claude names the host to allow
  • Changed Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle to use the shorter system prompt for model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names and inference profile ARNs, even when they front Sonnet or Haiku; set CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 to keep the full prompt
  • Changed automatic model switches after a flagged message to also cover model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_REFUSAL_FALLBACK=1 to turn them off
  • Changed usage limit messages to call the 5-hour window the "5-hour limit" instead of the "session limit"
  • Changed cloud sessions started from the CLI to get their names and branch names from the server
  • Changed prompt and agent hooks to run at most 24 at a time per session, sub-agents included, plus at most 12 that have waited longer than their event's timeout; a timeout under 1 second now counts as 1 second
  • Changed a subagent's autoCompactWindow to lower the window set by CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW, where it had no effect before; it still never raises that window
  • Changed OpenTelemetry mcp_server.name to report the real name of fixed-URL remote MCP servers declared by plugins from the official Anthropic marketplace, instead of custom
  • Changed Claude Code to stop sending the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event
  • [VSCode] Fixed sessions ending on a bare exit code when your organization's settings couldn't be loaded or were refused at startup; the tab now says why and offers Retry or Sign in again
  • [VSCode] Changed usage limit resets to show a clock time ("Resets at 3:10 PM") and to say "5-hour limit"
  • [Cloud sessions] Added an effort level to the model picker when you create or edit a routine that runs in the cloud
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Bash editor with colors, line numbers and a Copy button to the setup script box in cloud environment settings
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the step shown when Claude adds a repository to a cloud session: opening it now shows a short table of what happened instead of raw JSON
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed resending an unchanged message after a failed send in a cloud session sometimes running it twice
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed cloud environment creation showing its error only as a toast outside the open dialog; it now appears inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Edit in a routine's menu on the Routines page going to the routine's page without opening its edit dialog
  • [Remote Control] Fixed an unarchived Remote Control session showing as working until a computer reconnected; it now shows as idle
  • [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag's retry notice in Slack to name the model in use, or say rate limits were hit, instead of a generic API error
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a Claude Tag channel's on/off switch and agent settings falling back to workspace defaults when an older private Slack channel goes public and gets a new ID
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack not replying in channels whose environment has network access set to None
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes posting a file in the wrong thread when it was answering in another thread of the same channel
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review reviewing an outdated commit, or none at all, when GitHub delivered a push event late; it now reviews the pull request's current commit

items.title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
items.summary: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
items.story_key: model:glm|ver:5.3|title:cross request kv cache exposure in the glm 5 3 workers ai model and our remediat
items.content_excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic , to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue. The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the r
